summary: Documents a long-standing technique, supported by many mail servers, that tells users when new mail arrives. The server sends a short notification string to a client, which can alert the user or a mail client. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The mailman rings your doorbell to say a letter arrived, instead of you walking to check the mailbox. This memo describes that simple doorbell for email.

questions: how do mail servers notify of new mail
what is the biff finger hack
subtitle: A simple technique that tells a client when new mail arrives

tldr.problem: Users want to be notified immediately when new mail arrives, rather than constantly checking their mailbox.
tldr.mechanism: When new mail arrives, the mail server sends the text 'nm_notifyuser' followed by a line break to TCP port 79 (the finger port) on a client machine that is listening. A process on the client receives this and alerts a mail client to check for new mail.
tldr.outcome: This technique has been supported by many mail servers and clients for years and is now formally documented, allowing broader implementation.

today: RFC 4146 is a practical documentation of a technique that was already in widespread use. The technique remains in use today, though modern push notification systems have largely replaced it for mobile mail clients. The protocol is simple and low-overhead, making it suitable for systems that need immediate notification with minimal overhead.

sections.title: An Undocumented But Common Technique
sections.content: For years, mail servers have supported a simple way to notify users of new mail: the server sends a notification string to the user's client machine. RFC 4146 documents this long-standing practice, known by several names: 'notify mail' (after a shareware client), 'biff' (a Unix utility), or the 'finger hack.' Many mail servers and clients support it, but until this RFC, no specification existed. The RFC documents what the practice is, how it works, and what applications need to do to use it.
sections.eli5: This is describing something that people have been doing for years, but nobody wrote it down officially until now.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: When a user receives new mail, the mail server connects to port 79 (the finger port) on an IP address configured for the user (or the last IP address the user used to check mail from). It sends the string nm_notifyuser followed by a carriage return and line feed (CRLF), then closes the connection without waiting for a reply. On the client side, a process must be listening on port 79. When it receives the nm_notifyuser string, it takes a configured action, typically telling a mail client to fetch new mail. Most implementations use TCP for reliability, although some use UDP. The assumption is that the listening process handles only one email account, so it does not know which account received mail if it handles multiple accounts.
sections.eli5: Server sends a short message 'hey, new mail' to your computer's port 79. A program listening there wakes up a mail client to fetch the new messages.

sections.title: Example and Security
sections.content: The RFC includes a simple example: a client listening on TCP port 79 accepts a connection from the server. The server sends nm_notifyuser and CRLF and closes. The example shows that the setup assumes no finger daemon is running on the client (otherwise port 79 is already in use). Security considerations are important: there is no verification that the message came from a real mail server, so an attacker can send fake notifications. A malicious actor could flood a client with notifications. Applications listening on port 79 should implement flood protections and run with minimal privileges to limit the damage if the listening process has a vulnerability like a buffer overflow.
sections.eli5: It is a very simple system with security risks: attackers can fake the notification, and someone could spam you with false alerts. The client program should protect itself.
